query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the balance between mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch controls phase stability: near-equiatomic compositions maximize the free energy stabilization of a single FCC phase, thereby retaining high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness, whereas small systematic deviations (especially in Al and Ni content) shift the free energy balance to promote secondary-phase nucleation, which degrades these properties.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy exhibiting a single-phase FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the alloy’s composition by adjusting the relative concentrations of key elements (especially Al and Ni) away from the equiatomic baseline via combinatorial synthesis.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under high-temperature thermal cycling, controlled irradiation exposure, and cryogenic mechanical testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The modifications in the free energy landscape driven by changes in mixing enthalpy and atomic size misfit, thereby controlling the onset or suppression of secondary phases (e.g., intermetallic precipitates) within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Compositional deviations alter the alloy’s mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch, which in turn change the Gibbs free energy difference between the single-phase FCC state and potential multiphase states. When this balance is disrupted, secondary phases nucleate, adversely affecting properties such as high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness, as well as environmental and radiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The equiatomic alloy will maintain a stable, single FCC phase with optimal properties. In contrast, alloys with deliberately increased or decreased Al and/or Ni will show early signs (via synchrotron XRD and electron microscopy) of secondary-phase formation and concurrent degradation in mechanical and environmental properties.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy that maintains a single FCC phase and exhibits robust performance under high-temperature, irradiative, and cryogenic conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys produced under controlled synthesis and processing conditions. The predicted correlations may not hold if large compositional deviations or uncontrolled processing variations introduce structural inhomogeneities beyond the narrow compositional windows studied.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative relationships between the extent of compositional deviation, the corresponding shifts in mixing enthalpy/atomic size misfit, and the degree of property degradation remain to be determined. Additionally, effects from processing history and grain structure might modulate these trends.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys including an equiatomic baseline and variants with systematically varied Al and Ni concentrations. Use in situ synchrotron X‑ray diffraction and electron microscopy during high-temperature cycling, controlled irradiation tests, and cryogenic mechanical testing to monitor phase evolution and measure property changes.
measurements: Phase composition and secondary-phase volume fraction via XRD and microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If compositional variations (in Al and Ni) do not produce a measurable difference in phase stability (i.e., no emergence of secondary phases relative to the equiatomic baseline) and no correlated degradation in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, or cryogenic toughness is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Other prominent features distinguishing HEAs from CAs in a wide temperature range include sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion. The joint effects of these factors affect the corrosion resistance, tribocorrosion tendencies, strength, hardness, ductility, oxidation/wear, and erosion resistance. The determination of phase selection in HEAs is primarily rationalized based on statistically arranged thermodynamic ranges for most critical parameters. Additionally, researchers have highlighted that the high mixing entropy is a key factor resulting in the formation of HEA. Specifically, a high mixing entropy promotes the formation of solid solution phases by lowering the Gibbs free energy, as opposed to complex-structured phases such as intermetallic compounds. However, a statistical analysis of thermodynamic parameters for various HEAs has indicated that in addition to high mixing entropy, the atomic size difference (δ) and enthalpy of mixing (ΔHmix) influence the phase selection. While the yield strength and KJIc fracture toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi and high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloys are comparable, the tensile strengths, tensile ductility and work of fracture of the CrCoNi alloy are significantly higher, by respectively ∼15, ∼30 and ∼50%, at room temperature. At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths of the two alloys are comparable (σUTS∼1,300 MPa at 77 K), but the KJIc fracture toughness, tensile ductility and work of fracture are again markedly higher in the CrCoNi alloy, by ∼25, ∼27 and ∼31%, respectively. The yield strength, σy, at 77 K is slightly below that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which we believe is due to the non-uniform grain size of our present material (Fig. 1b–d). Consistent with this notion, in a previous study where the grain size of CrCoNi was uniform and comparable to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, the tensile properties of the three-component alloy were found to exceed those of the five-component alloy at all temperatures.

chosen.technique: combinatorial synthesis combined with in situ synchrotron X‐ray diffraction and electron microscopy
chosen.conditions: testing a matrix of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys where key element concentrations are varied relative to an equiatomic baseline, under high-temperature cycling, irradiation exposure, and cryogenic mechanical testing
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by experimentally isolating the role of compositional variations in governing phase stability. By systematically altering the relative concentrations of the constituent elements, the study predicts that deviations in mixing enthalpy and atomic size misfit will modulate the free energy landscape to favor or suppress secondary phase formation. The chosen experimental conditions span the regimes relevant to high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness, and the techniques are standard in the field. Moreover, the hypothesis is falsifiable if no systematic shifts in phase stability or property degradation are observed relative to the established baseline.
